query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of a ductility‐enhancing element (e.g. ~2 at.% titanium) to NbMoTaW will induce the formation of a minor ductile FCC or nanodomain phase that activates additional slip systems (and possibly promotes twinning) at room temperature, thereby improving ductility without degrading the high-temperature BCC matrix responsible for the 1600 °C mechanical strength or compromising irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and 1600 °C, together with irradiation exposure tests under conditions representative of service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a controlled, minor amount of a ductile FCC or nanophase (e.g., twin-rich) precipitate dispersed within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The added Ti is expected to lower the stacking fault energy locally and promote twinning or activate additional slip systems. This localized phase change improves dislocation mobility and promotes twinning-induced plasticity at room temperature, while the dominant BCC matrix remains intact to preserve high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-microalloyed alloy is predicted to show significantly improved room-temperature ductility (i.e. increased elongation/plastic strain), while maintaining similar tensile strength and yield behavior at 1600 °C and comparable irradiation-induced microstructural stability.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with poor room-temperature ductility but high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low-level Ti additions; excessive Ti could lead to an undesirable increase in the ductile phase fraction that might weaken high-temperature strength or alter irradiation response.
generation.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction of the secondary phase induced by Ti and its influence on both room-temperature ductility and high-temperature performance remain uncertain without detailed microstructural and phase stability studies. The optimum Ti content to balance these properties is also not yet precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples – one set as the baseline (without Ti) and one with ~2 at.% Ti addition. Process both sets under identical conditions. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature to measure ductility (elongation to failure) and at 1600 °C to check high-temperature strength. Expose samples to controlled irradiation conditions and subsequently assess microstructural stability and mechanical properties.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Irradiation damage assessment (e.g., defect density, microstructural changes via TEM/SEM)
Phase analysis (XRD, TEM) to quantify the presence and distribution of any secondary (FCC or twin-rich) phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility while maintaining similar high-temperature tensile properties and irradiation resistance as the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified. In particular, if Ti addition leads to a significant deterioration in high-temperature performance or irradiation-induced stability, the hypothesis will be deemed invalid.

AbstractThe as-cast [Co40Cr25(FeNi)35−yMoy]100−xCx (x = 0, 0.5, y = 3, 4, 5 at.%) HEAs (high-entropy alloys) were prepared by a vacuum arc melting furnace and were then hot rolled. The effect of C and Mo elements on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of HEAs was systematically analyzed. The results showed that when no C atoms were added, the HEAs consisted of FCC + HCP dual-phase structure. In addition, as the Mo content increased, the grain size of the alloy increased from 17 μm to 47 μm. However, only the FCC phase appeared after adding 0.5 at.% carbon in Mo microalloyed HEAs, and the grain size of the Mo4C0.5 HEA decreased significantly. Due to the Mo atom content exceeding the solid solution limit, the carbides of Mo combined with the C element appeared in the Mo5C0.5 HEA. The strength of C and Mo microalloyed HEAs significantly increased compared to HEAs with no C added. However, the Mo4C0.5 HEA exhibited excellent comprehensive mechanical properties, which was superior to a majority of reported HEAs and conventional metal alloys.
